# Draw and Paint Art

This craft skill owns 2D drawing and digital painting: gesture, construction, anatomy, light, colour, Krita and Grease Pencil.
`2d-generalist`, `3d-generalist`, `model-characters` and `use-3d-software` call it. They keep the look and the order of work.

## When to use

- You draw or paint a figure, a character, a prop or a painted texture.
- You build a turnaround, pose sheet or style sheet that a 3D artist will model from.
- You review a figure or sheet for anatomy, proportion, pose and silhouette errors.
- You set up Krita or Blender Grease Pencil for drawing.

## Ask first

When the user calls this skill directly for a new piece, find out what they want before you make anything. Read the
request, attachments and project files, then ask only about what is still unclear and would change the result:
purpose and platform, format (aspect, length, file type), subject details, look (style, references) and constraints.
Ask at most 4 questions in one round, each with 2 to 4 concrete options and your recommended option first (Claude Code:
`AskUserQuestion`; elsewhere a numbered list where "ok" takes the first options). Restate the goal in 2 or 3 lines,
show the cheapest preview of the look before the expensive step, and compare the result with the goal before you hand
it over. When a generalist skill called this one with a brief, use that brief and do not ask again.

## Core rules

1. Start with flow. Draw one line of action (a long S or C curve through neck and spine) before any shape.
2. Build every form from simple volumes. Use two blocks for ribcage and pelvis, cylinders for limbs, a circle at each joint and a box or ellipse for the head.
3. Draw through the forms. Draw the hidden edges so the parts do not contradict each other.
4. Work rough to clean. Lower the sketch layer opacity, trace once or twice with a darker line, and ink last.
5. Tilt the ribcage and pelvis against each other for contrapposto. Check head size against the ribcage.
6. Parts that come toward the viewer get bigger. A limb that tapers toward a joint can shrink as it comes forward.
7. Light has one direction. Paint in order: core shadow, light side, highlight, reflected light (lighter than the core shadow, darker than the lit side), cast shadow.
8. Paint values first in grayscale. Add colour with Color layers, Overlay and a Gradient Map, and keep the colours in value order.
9. Make the front line thicker where two shapes overlap, and avoid tangents between outlines.
10. Check the silhouette and the negative space. A strong silhouette is the goal in any style.
11. Shape language sets the feeling: circle is friendly, square is solid, triangle is aggressive. This holds for any style.
12. Flip the canvas often. A mirrored view shows errors that you stopped seeing.

## Workflow

1. Name the style and the use (concept, texture, sheet, final art). Pick the reference (3D pose viewer, photo, source model).
2. Draw the gesture and line of action, then the block-in (two blocks, limbs, joints, head).
3. Check proportion and pose on the block-in before adding anatomy or detail.
4. Add anatomy and surface forms, then the clean line pass with varied line weight.
5. Paint values in grayscale, then colour.
6. For 3D, export the sheet or texture and hand it to `model-characters` or `use-3d-software`.
7. Run the checks below.

## Routing

| The task is | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Gesture, line of action, construction, poses from reference, line weight | references/gesture-and-construction.md |
| Anatomy of torso, arm, leg, hand, foot, head, foreshortening, proportion checks | references/anatomy-and-foreshortening.md |
| Painting light on a form, colouring, painterly texture, portrait workflow | references/light-form-and-colour.md |
| Krita menus, dockers, brushes, layers, blending modes, Alpha Lock, transform | references/krita-and-tools.md |
| Grease Pencil v3 in Blender: drawing, layers, fills, Line Art, 2D over 3D | references/grease-pencil-drawing.md |
| Turnaround or style sheets, cut-out parts, painting textures for 3D | references/character-sheets-for-3d.md |
| Noticing, detail comparison, grayscale value check, final attack checklist, composition and colour variety | references/noticing-and-design-lessons.md |
| Paint over a Blender render, fake depth with paint | references/light-form-and-colour.md |
| Illustration stage order: sketch, sculpt, pose, props, light, paint-over | references/illustration-process-2d-3d.md |

For UV unwrap, seams, Texture Paint and rigging steps, use `model-characters` and `use-3d-software`. Do not copy those steps here.

## Checks

- Hide the sketch layer. The pose must still read from the silhouette alone.
- Flip the canvas horizontally and squint. Fix any lean, wrong head size or uneven shoulders.
- Compare head size with the ribcage, and compare limb lengths on both sides.
- Make a grayscale copy. The value order (dark, mid, light) must show the form and the light direction.
- Check each overlap and tangent in the line art.
- For a character sheet, overlay the views at the same scale. Heights, joints and key landmarks must line up across front, side and back.
- Save the file with layers (.kra) next to the flat export.
- Run the final attack checklist in `references/noticing-and-design-lessons.md` before you hand a piece over.

# Edit Video

A tool skill. The generalist skills (`2d-generalist`, `3d-generalist`) decide the story, the look and the order of
work. This skill says how to cut, time, finish and export the video in the editor the user has, by exact UI path,
by script or by command.

## When to use

- Cutting footage or renders into a piece, a Short or a reel, with captions, music, transitions and effects.
- A retime, title, grade, composite or export in any editor, or a batch job with FFmpeg.
- Not for building video in code (Remotion) and not for designing sound. Mix levels here, design sound elsewhere.

## Pick the editor

Use the editor the user already has. When nothing decides it: DaVinci Resolve for a full edit with effects and grade
(the free edition covers most work); CapCut for a fast phone-first Short with auto captions; FFmpeg for batch,
scripted or headless jobs; Kdenlive or Shotcut when the user wants open source; Premiere and After Effects when the
user already pays for them. Ask before suggesting a paid tool.

## Routing

# Paint Stylized Backgrounds

This craft skill owns stylized background art: the base render or photo, the paint-over, the light, the colour variants and the motion in the background.
`2d-generalist`, `3d-generalist`, `use-3d-software` and `edit-video` call it. They keep the look and the order of the whole project.

## When to use

- A film, Short, game scene or illustration needs a painted or stylized background plate.
- You must turn a Blender render or a photo into a painted background.
- One background must work at day, evening, night and in rain.
- A still background must move: parallax, wind, water, birds, fireworks, card shine.

## Ask first

When the user calls this skill directly for a new piece, find out what they want before you make anything. Read the
request, attachments and project files, then ask only about what is still unclear and would change the result:
purpose and platform, format (aspect, length, file type), subject details, look (style, references) and constraints.
Ask at most 4 questions in one round, each with 2 to 4 concrete options and your recommended option first (Claude Code:
`AskUserQuestion`; elsewhere a numbered list where "ok" takes the first options). Restate the goal in 2 or 3 lines,
show the cheapest preview of the look before the expensive step, and compare the result with the goal before you hand
it over. When a generalist skill called this one with a brief, use that brief and do not ask again.

## Core rules

1. Render the base in Blender EEVEE with View Transform = Standard. Filmic and AgX grey out flat colours. Use AgX only for stylized realistic.
2. Choose the base by the place. Use a photo for a real location. Use a render for a made-up place. Block out simple shapes and paint more, or model more and paint less.
3. Paint the base bright, in daytime light, without hard shadows. Redraw shadows for each mood on their own layers.
4. Split the art into foreground, middle ground and background layers before you colour or animate. Paint behind every occlusion so the parallax has no holes.
5. Soften the CG edge first: draw lighter bevel lines on object edges and roughen shadow and glow edges. Do this on every object, not on some.
6. Build depth with fog on a clipped layer. Far layers get lighter and lower in contrast. Near layers stay darker and sharper.
7. Use warm light with cool or blue shadows. Tint the dark world colour, because some shadows still go grey. Ghibli-like style uses a yellow-green fill instead of cold blue.
8. Repaint the sky for each mood. A photo filter on the sky looks wrong.
9. Remove frozen people and animals from a plate that will move.
10. Add noise (Overlay or Soft Light) on top to hide the seam between photo, render and paint. Skip it for flat cartoon.
11. Move far layers slower than near layers. Vary every value in a copy so wind and sway never run in sync.
12. Keep a clean daytime master and build every variant from it.
13. In a Blender background, cut clouds and mountains as image cards with a mask, fade far cards bluer, add a fog plane, and tie everything with one low-strength compositor tint.

## Workflow

1. Choose the base (photo, blockout render or detailed render) and the style. Read `references/render-and-blockout.md`.
2. Render with Standard colour, a transparent film and simple lights. Keep passes and layers you need for the paint-over.
3. Crop, fix the perspective, split into layers, then adjust colour. Read `references/paint-over-and-brushes.md`.
4. Paint over: edges, sky, clouds, trees, grass, removals. Add glow, rays, fog and grain.
5. Build the time-of-day and weather variants. Read `references/light-colour-and-time-of-day.md`.
6. Animate: parallax first, then wind, water and other moving elements. Read `references/animate-backgrounds.md`.
7. Run the checks below, then hand the plate to the calling skill.

| Parallax, camera moves, wind, foliage, water, birds, fireworks, holographic card | `references/animate-backgrounds.md` |

| Leaf planes, Sapling trees, bushes, anime grass, falling leaves, foliage wind | `references/blender-foliage-and-grass.md` |

For NPR toon shading, outlines and painted character textures, read `model-characters` `references/npr-shading-and-painted-look.md`. Do not copy those steps here.

## Checks

- Look at the plate at full size and at thumbnail size. The layers must read far to near.
- Check the colours: no grey wash, no pure black shadows, no clipped glow.
- Check every layer edge for a halo, a hole or a cropped corner after the camera move.

- Compare the day, evening and night variants side by side. Light sources must stay brighter than their surroundings.
- Check that the style rule held: a flat cartoon plate has no grain, a Ghibli-like plate has soft edges.

# 3D Generalist

Act as a complete 3D creative studio for content creators. Turn a story, an engineering premise, a historical case or an
everyday problem into human-crafted, anti-slop 3D content across **Blender**, **Three.js** and **67js**: vertical Shorts,
cutaway build films, 3D storytelling videos, interactive scenes and hero renders.

# Animate Characters in 2D and 3D

This craft skill owns the motion of a character, creature or prop: poses, timing, curves, cycles and face swaps.
`3d-generalist`, `2d-generalist`, `model-characters` and `use-3d-software` call it.
They keep the look and the order of the whole job. For building the rig, use the `rig-characters` skill.

## When to use

- A character, creature or prop must move with weight, acting or a loop.
- A motion looks stiff, floaty, robotic or "on rails", and you must fix the cause.
- You need a walk, run or idle cycle, a face swap, or a hand-drawn sequence.
- Not for camera moves, NLA layering or Blender recipes: see
  [use-3d-software animation-and-nla](../use-3d-software/references/animation-and-nla.md).

## Ask first

When the user calls this skill directly for a new piece, find out what they want before you make anything. Read the
request, attachments and project files, then ask only about what is still unclear and would change the result:
purpose and platform, format (aspect, length, file type), subject details, look (style, references) and constraints.
Ask at most 4 questions in one round, each with 2 to 4 concrete options and your recommended option first (Claude Code:
`AskUserQuestion`; elsewhere a numbered list where "ok" takes the first options). Restate the goal in 2 or 3 lines,
show the cheapest preview of the look before the expensive step, and compare the result with the goal before you hand
it over. When a generalist skill called this one with a brief, use that brief and do not ask again.

## Core rules

1. Work pose to pose. Block the key poses first, then breakdowns, then in-betweens. Use straight ahead only for fire, smoke and loose masses.
2. Block on Constant (stepped) in 3D and on holds in 2D. Switch to Bezier only after the timing reads.
3. Every action gets an anticipation, a small opposite move 3 to 6 frames before it. Realistic styles keep it small, cartoon styles push it.
4. The head leads every turn and notice by 4 to 6 frames. Never stop all joints on one frame: stagger the stops 3 to 6 frames apart.
5. Attached parts (hair, tail, cloth, ears) lag the main mass by 1 to 3 frames. They overshoot at the stop, about 3 frames later.
6. Spacing makes weight. Put the keys close together near the poses (slow in, slow out) and far apart in the fast middle. A fall is faster than a rise.
7. Limbs travel on arcs. Check them with motion paths in 3D and with a drawn path line in 2D. IK paths need breakdown keys to bend.
8. Squash and stretch conserve volume: stretch along the force, squash across it, and keep the contact frame for 2 frames.
9. Pick the pose by silhouette. Hide the interior and check that the pose still reads. Avoid tangents between outlines.
10. Retime with `S` then `X` (timing only). Plain `S` in the Graph Editor scales the values and warps the pose.
11. A loop needs an identical first and last pose, and the last frame is the one before the first. Otherwise the loop pops.
12. Judge timing only at real speed (Sync to Audio, 24 fps with motion blur or on twos). Play it many times between edits.

## Workflow

1. Plan the action in words: beats, the idea of each pose, the length in seconds. Gather a reference clip when the action is real.
2. Choose the tool and the frame rate. 24 fps with motion blur, 30 fps for games, on twos for hand-drawn or stylized work.
3. Pick IK or FK per shot (see the `cycles-and-locomotion.md` entry). Hide the controls you do not need.
4. Block the key poses on Constant. Check each from front and side in orthographic view.
5. Set the timing: hold frames, anticipation and the spacing. Preview the range (`P`) at real speed.
6. Add breakdowns. Fix arcs and weight shift. Then switch to Bezier or add in-betweens.
7. Add overlap, follow through and secondary action as a separate pass or layer.
8. Add face swaps and blinks, then procedural noise or wiggle on the loose parts.
9. Playblast with overlays, run the checks below, then hand back to the calling skill.

## Checks

- Scrub frame by frame. Look for pops at cut points, foot slide and joints that freeze on the same frame.
- Turn on motion paths and look at the wrists, feet and head. Fix any straight or kinked path.
- Play the loop twice in a row. The seam must not show.
- Hide the mesh or fill the shape black. The silhouette must show the action.
- Play at real speed with sound. If it feels floaty, shorten the in-betweens. If it feels robotic, offset the stops.
- For a face swap, step through the frames. Each face must change in one frame, with no blend.
- Render a low resolution playblast of the whole shot before any full render.
- Stepped style: the character, shaders, outline boil and effects all use one step size. Check the Dope Sheet for keys on
  every 2 or 3 frames.

# Model 3D Characters
Paths use `{{WORK_DIR}}` for the project folder and `{{SKILL_DIR}}` for this skill's folder.

If `references/local.md` exists, read it first for local paths and machine rules.

A craft skill. It turns a reference (drawing, turnaround, photo, text idea) into a 3D character in the style the user
wants. Low poly is one route, not the default. The generalist skills (`3d-generalist`, `2d-generalist`) decide the
story and the shot. This skill decides how the character is built. Tool-specific steps live in `use-3d-software`.

## Ask first

When the user calls this skill directly for a new piece, find out what they want before you make anything. Read the
request, attachments and project files, then ask only about what is still unclear and would change the result:
purpose and platform, format (game asset, film, still, print), subject details, look (style, references) and
constraints (triangle budget, engine, deadline). Ask at most 4 questions in one round, each with 2 to 4 concrete
options and your recommended option first (Claude Code: `AskUserQuestion`; elsewhere a numbered list where "ok" takes
the first options). Restate the goal in 2 or 3 lines, show the cheapest preview of the look (a blockout still or a
turnaround grey render) before the expensive step, and compare the result with the goal before you hand it over.
When a generalist skill called this one with a brief, use that brief and do not ask again.

## Pick the route

| The character should be | Route | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Low poly: PS1, N64, chibi, anime, mascot, painterly, under about 2k triangles | Low-poly | `references/style-presets.md`, then `references/low-poly-route.md` |
| Stylized and smooth: cartoon, Pixar-like, figurine, toy, collectible | Sculpt | `references/sculpt-stylized.md`, then retopo by the base-mesh route; anatomy, creatures, surface detail, bake and the silhouette check: the `sculpt-models` skill |
| Clean quads for subdivision, a game LOD or a sculpt base | Base mesh | `references/base-mesh-and-box-modeling.md` |
| Realistic human or creature | Generate or source, then adapt | `3d-generalist` `references/characters-and-rigs.md` (generators, scans, Mixamo, retargeting); for close-ups generate in parts and bake: `sculpt-models` `references/ai-mesh-to-game-ready.md` |
| Anime-semireal, painted or manga character, finished by painting and rendered in EEVEE | Painted | `references/stylized-character-process.md` (build order, head, body, hair), then `references/npr-shading-and-painted-look.md` |
| Toon shader, key and rim light, Solidify outline, painted mask layers or hatching on any model | Shading | `references/npr-shading-and-painted-look.md` (shared with the background and animation skills) |
| An existing model to restyle | Adapt | Keep the rig if it has one. Repaint by `uv-and-texturing.md`, reshape by the sculpt route |

Prefer a licence-clear base (CC0 or CC BY scans, generator output, an open base mesh) over modelling a realistic
human from nothing. Credit it.

## Steps for every route

1. **Measure the reference.** For a turnaround or front view, run
   `uv run --no-project {{SKILL_DIR}}/scripts/read_character_ref.py ref.png --height 1.70 --out cal`.
   It gives head count, joint heights, width and depth profiles and a colour palette. For a single sketch, set the
   height and the head count by hand and write them down.
2. **Block out** the silhouette in large parts at the measured heights. Check front, side and three-quarter views
   against the reference before any detail. Read `references/head-and-face.md` before the head.
3. **Build the route.** Follow the route file. Keep scale applied, mirror on the centre line, and parts separate
   where clothing or hair makes a step in the silhouette.
4. **Topology for motion.** Add loops at the knees, elbows, shoulders, mouth and eyes when the character will bend.
   A sculpt that must animate is retopologized or decimated first.
5. **UV and texture.** `references/uv-and-texturing.md` for atlases, unlit colour and ramps. Hand-painted and
   stylized painting craft is in `draw-and-paint-art`.
6. **Rig and animate.** Hand off to `rig-characters` and `animate-characters`. The short low-poly rig notes are in
   `references/rigging-and-animation.md`.
7. **Check.** Run `uv run --no-project {{SKILL_DIR}}/scripts/check_character.py character.glb --max-tris <budget>`
   on the export, then render a turnaround still and compare it with the reference side by side.

## More references

- `references/modeling-and-topology.md`: part-by-part low-poly recipes in Blender, three.js and 67js.
- `references/more-build-methods.md`: Wind Waker style head, cylinder bodies, clothes as shells, hats, face atlas.
- `references/npr-shading-and-painted-look.md`: toon shader, two-sun rim rig, outlines, painted layers, bake.
- `references/stylized-character-process.md`: painted character build order, head, hands, hair, design lessons.
- `references/stylized-modeling-and-texture-painting.md`: cute cartoon builds from a subdivided cube or round cube, clothes as shells, curve tubes, metaball hair, face discs, round chibi bodies and loose-edge faces, carved Boolean faces, topology fixes, texture-paint layers, VDM brushes.
- `references/faults.md`: geometry, UV, rig and animation faults and their fixes.
- `use-3d-software`: the exact steps per tool (Blender sculpt and modifiers, export to three.js, Godot, Unity, Unreal).

## Hard rules

- No box head and no flat face plate. The face has a nose, brow and cheek steps in the side view.
- UV before texture. Never project at a harsh camera angle.
- No internal or coplanar faces. Delete caps inside open cylinders and along mirror seams.
- Skinned vertices have normalized weights (sum 1.0, at most 4 influences for engines).
- Bend knees and elbows slightly in the rest pose when the rig uses IK.
- Stepped (`Constant`) keys on UV-offset face controllers.
- Run `uv run --no-project {{SKILL_DIR}}/scripts/test_character_skill.py` after changing any script in `scripts/`.

# Rig Characters

This skill owns the rigging method: skeleton, skinning, controls, face rigs and engine export. `3d-generalist`, `2d-generalist`,
`model-characters` and `use-3d-software` call it. They own the look and the order of work.

## When to use

- A mesh or a set of drawn parts must move under control, and the rig is not built yet.
- A rig deforms badly: pinched joints, a reversed elbow, a hand that follows the wrong bone.
- A face needs expressions: bones, shape keys or a texture atlas.
- A rigid machine needs joints without a skeleton.
- A rig must work in Unity (Mecanim), Godot, three.js, 67js or glTF.

Exact Blender button recipes are in `use-3d-software/references/rigging-and-weights.md`. Read it for those steps.
This skill adds the method around them and the other tools.

## Ask first

When the user calls this skill directly for a new piece, find out what they want before you make anything. Read the
request, attachments and project files, then ask only about what is still unclear and would change the result:
purpose and platform, format (aspect, length, file type), subject details, look (style, references) and constraints.
Ask at most 4 questions in one round, each with 2 to 4 concrete options and your recommended option first (Claude Code:
`AskUserQuestion`; elsewhere a numbered list where "ok" takes the first options). Restate the goal in 2 or 3 lines,
show the cheapest preview of the look before the expensive step, and compare the result with the goal before you hand
it over. When a generalist skill called this one with a brief, use that brief and do not ask again.

## Core rules

1. Apply the Mirror modifier and the object scale before you rig. Both sides need real geometry and scale must be 1.
2. Put every joint where the character really bends, inside the mesh. A wrong joint is the main cause of bad deformation.
3. Keep a slight bend in elbows and knees (knees forward, elbows back). IK reads the bend direction from it.
4. Name left bones with a `.L` suffix, build one side, then Symmetrize. Put `IK` in control bone names so search finds them.
5. Test bone roll with a local X rotation on every limb and finger. Do it before IK or Generate.
6. Turn Deform off on every control, IK, pole and root bone before you skin. Only the real skeleton deforms.
7. Clear the parent of IK and pole bones. A leftover parent link breaks the IK chain.
8. Skin with automatic weights first, then fix by hand with low strength. Test by rotating bones, not by reading colours.
9. Never add or delete geometry after shape keys exist. Change the Basis first.
10. Parent rigid accessories (shoes, hair, teeth) to a deform bone, never to a control bone.
11. Use IK for planted contacts and FK for loose drag. Keep both on one rig with a switch.
12. Test a rig that leaves Blender in the target engine with one stock clip before you call it done.

## Workflow

1. Pick the rig type: Rigify biped, custom armature, mechanical (no bones), shape keys only, or 2D cut-out.
2. Prepare the mesh: apply Mirror and scale, put the feet on the ground at the world origin, centre the character.
3. Build the skeleton and fit it. Check roll and left/right names.
4. Add controls: root, IK with pole targets, IK/FK switch, foot roll, and bone collections that hide helpers.
5. Skin: automatic weights, then hard weights for rigid parts, then paint fixes.
6. Add the face rig if the shot needs one.
7. Pose a stress test: a run pose, a fist, arms overhead, a deep knee bend. Fix pinching.
8. Export or hand off. Test in the target engine.

## Routing

| The task is | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Bone naming, meta-rig fitting, Rigify generation, roll, automatic and hard weights, weight fixes | `references/bones-and-weights.md` |
| IK with pole targets, IK/FK choice and switching, snapping, bone collections, ready rigs | `references/ik-fk-and-controls.md` |
| Shape keys, eye and mouth bones, 2D face atlas driven by a bone, blinking | `references/face-rigs.md` |
| A robot arm or machine without bones, a 2D cut-out puppet from Krita layers | `references/mechanical-and-cutout.md` |
| Rig to Unity Mecanim, Godot, three.js, 67js, glTF | `references/export-to-engines.md` |
| A creature spine with controller bones, bendy bones, IK legs, Damped Track tails, Rigify frog or custom face, wind on bones, Bake Action | `references/creature-and-stylized-rigs.md` |
| Stylized recipes: image-sequence faces, Rigify samples for non-humanoids, rubber-hose and squash rigs, hard-weight toy rigs, ragdoll proxies, eye rigs | `references/stylized-rig-recipes.md` |
| A character holds, picks up, carries, hands over or puts down a prop; two-handed props; grip, weight, fingers; any software | `references/props-grip-and-contact.md` |
| Exact Blender menu steps for any of the above | `use-3d-software/references/rigging-and-weights.md` |

## Checks

- Rotate every limb and finger by 90 degrees. No candy-wrapper twist, no pinched elbow, no mesh left behind.
- Reset the pose (Alt+G, Alt+R, Alt+S in Blender). The mesh returns to the rest shape.
- Mirror a pose. The other side matches, and the pole angles on `.R` are right.
- Move the root and the hips. The whole rig and the legs follow.
- In Weight Paint, only deform bones show weights. Control bones show the mesh pink.
- Shape-key face: set every key to 1 once and nothing explodes. Set all to 0 and the Basis returns.
- Export: load the file in the target engine and play one clip. Watch the feet, the hands and the scale.

# Sculpt Models

This craft skill owns digital sculpting: form, anatomy, surface detail, environment sculpts and the Blender 5.x
sculpt toolset, through to a retopologised and baked asset. It is called by `3d-generalist` and `model-characters`.
Read `local.md` next to this file when it exists (machine paths).

## When to use

- A character, creature, head or bust that must read as organic, not blobby or symmetric.
- Rocks, cliffs, terrain, bark, ruins, worn and damaged props.
- Refining an AI base mesh (Tripo Studio) or a scanned mesh: re-cutting planes, eyelids, mouth corners, folds.
- A realistic close-up asset from AI: generate in parts, retopo, bake to a low poly (`references/ai-mesh-to-game-ready.md`).
- Turning one picture (AI image, render, figurine photo, drawing) into a sculpt measured against it.
- Baking sculpt detail onto a low-poly mesh for a game engine, three.js or 67js.

Not this skill: stylised cartoon character sculpts step by step (`~/.claude/skills/model-characters/references/sculpt-stylized.md`),
machined parts at exact dimensions (`model-parts-in-cad`), drawing anatomy in 2D (`draw-and-paint-art`).

## Order of work

1. **Reference first.** Real photos or scans of the subject from several views (the `real resources first` rule):
   an animal, a rock type, a face type. Never sculpt a real thing from memory.
2. **Decide the end state.** Static (prop, environment, still) or deforming (rigged, animated); target face count and
   where it ships (`references/blender-sculpt-tools.md`, "Retopology and bake"). This decides every later step.
3. **Block out primary forms** from simple volumes at real scale, symmetry on, 5k to 20k faces, Voxel Remesh to unify.
   Run `scripts/check_sculpt.py` and read the silhouette sheet before any detail.
4. **Secondary forms:** planes, landmarks, muscle groups, folds, fracture planes (`references/form-and-anatomy.md`,
   `references/surfaces-environment-and-hard-surface.md`).
5. **Break symmetry** for anything alive, then **Multires** for tertiary detail in distinct layers by scale.
6. **Retopologise or decimate, then bake** normals (and displacement where detail changes the silhouette).
7. **Check again** (below) at the final camera distance, then hand the asset to `rig-characters` or the scene.

## Hard rules

- Big to small, always. No detail on a form whose silhouette has not passed.
- No global noise displace on a primitive as "sculpting": masses are built as volumes first.
- No perfect mirror on anything alive; no random vertex jitter as "asymmetry".
- Detail comes in distinct scales with rest areas between; one-frequency noise everywhere fails.
- Eyes, lids, lips, ears and nostrils have thickness and structure (`references/form-and-anatomy.md` §2).
- A sculpt that must deform is retopologised; a static one may be decimated. Never rig raw Dyntopo or voxel topology.
- Apply scale before sculpting; a scaled object stretches every stroke.

## Check gate (run before showing anyone)

```
blender -b <file.blend> --python scripts/check_sculpt.py -- [--object Name] [--out <folder>]
blender -b --python scripts/check_sculpt.py -- --import model.glb --out <folder>
```

It prints faces, scale, non-manifold edges, loose vertices, mirror error and surface busyness, and writes a
silhouette sheet (8 angles plus top and bottom) and a matcap and studio sheet. Exit 1 means a measured check failed.
Then look (more than about 5 pictures go through a frame-reading subagent):

1. The silhouette reads as the subject from every angle, at thumbnail size.
2. Under the raking studio light, forms are planes and landmarks, not mush; nothing is lumpy noise.
3. Squint: only primary and secondary forms remain, with a clear value pattern.
4. Flip the front view horizontally: proportion and tilt errors pop out.
5. At the final output size, delete detail nobody will see; keep what reads.

Tests: `bash tests/test_check_sculpt.sh` (a clean fixture passes, a broken one fails on scale and a loose vertex).
Worked procedural example: `blender -b --python scripts/procedural_rock.py -- --out rock.blend` (joint-set cuts, corner chips, masked layered displacement, QuadriFlow or Decimate low copy).

# Use 3D Software

A tool skill. The generalist and craft skills decide what to make. This one says how to do it in the tool the user
has or the target needs, by script or by the exact UI path, with current names.

## When to use

- Any step inside a 3D app or engine: a node tree, a material, a rig, a modifier stack, a bake, a headless render,
  an import, a scene in an engine, an export to another tool.
- Called from `3d-generalist`, `2d-generalist`, `model-characters`, `rig-characters`, `animate-characters`,
  `draw-and-paint-art` and `paint-stylized-backgrounds`. They own the workflow and the look. Do not restate their steps.
- Not for hard-surface CAD with exact dimensions (use a CAD tool such as build123d or FreeCAD).

## Pick the tool

Use the tool the user already has or the delivery needs. When nothing decides it: Blender for modeling, rigging,
offline renders and film; three.js for a page people open in a browser; Godot for a free, light game; Unity for a
mobile or cross-platform game with a big asset store; Unreal for a photoreal real-time scene or game.

## Routing

| The task is | Read |
|---|---|
| Any Blender step: headless runs, priority, version names | `references/blender-headless-and-versions.md` first |

| Blender lighting roles and ratios, light linking, IES and gobos, cheap fog, Cycles and EEVEE speed, 2.5D backgrounds, scatter and LOD in geometry nodes, hotkeys | `references/lighting-render-and-gn-recipes.md` |

Read the reading map at the top of a reference, then the full entry you use. Entries keep exact steps and a source
link. Open the source link only when an entry is thin.

## Move assets between tools

- GLB (glTF 2.0) is the default between Blender, three.js, 67js and Godot. FBX is the default into Unity and Unreal.
  USD for big scenes and Omniverse or SimReady assets.
- Apply scale and rotation before export. Blender is Z up. glTF, three.js, Godot and Unity are Y up. Unreal is Z up
  in centimetres. Check the forward axis on the first import with a test cube and an arrow.
- Bake procedural materials and modifiers that the target cannot read. Keep textures power of two.
- Name armature bones consistently. Export one action per clip, or split clips on import.
- Re-import into the target and look at it there before calling it done.

## How to work

1. Find the entry. If several fit, take the one closest to the installed version and note any renamed item.
2. Prefer a script for anything repeatable. Use the UI path when the user wants to learn or edit by hand.
3. Build in the smallest scene that shows the technique, then swap in the real asset.
4. Prefer a real asset from a licence-clear source (Poly Haven, ambientCG, Kenney, Quaternius) and credit it. For a
   restricted or unknown licence, ask the user once: use it at their responsibility, or skip it.
5. Name nodes, groups and objects. Expose inputs the user will tune.

## Checks before handing off

- Render or run one frame in the target tool and read the picture, not the node tree or the code.
- Look for stretched textures (unapplied scale), flipped normals, z-fighting, wrong axis, missing textures,
  black or grey colour from a wrong colour space, and popping at a loop point.
- For a rig, pose the extremes. For a loop, compare the first and last frames. For a script, run it twice.
- Paid add-ons and packs in the references are sources of ideas. Never buy or add one without the user's say.
- Report which entries and renamed items you used, and what you saw in the frame.
